nodes.title: Revisions
nodes.body:
January 19, 1993.  T.D. Phillips; Mote Marine Laboratory
FLELMR CODE: 1624

Scientific Name: Caranx crysos
Common Name: Blue Runner
OTHER COMMON NAMES: Jager boca, Bau, Deep water cavally; cavally, yellow mackerel (834); crevalle, hard tail, runner (312 834); horse crevalle, jurel, olbacore (834).

nodes.title: CLASSIFICATION
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
	Class: Osteichthyes
	Order: Perciformes
	Family: Carangidae

nodes.title: VALUE
nodes.body:
Commercial: Blue runner is the most commercially important species of the jacks. A small historic fishery existed in the Chesapeake Bay, and along the Gulf Coast it has been reported to be ?esteemed as food? (312 834). Annual landings of blue runner in the northeast Gulf of Mexico are approximately 600 metric tons (804). The largest catches occur in the northwest and southeast coasts of Florida and off the Louisiana coast. Florida landings totaled 1.4 million pounds worth nearly $275,600 in 1982, with approximately 88% landed off the Florida west coast (902). Much of the Florida catch is used for bait, but some is sold fresh as food (791 1048). Beach and haul seines are the primary gear used to exploit blue runner (791). In Puerto Rico, Trinidad, and the West Indies, blue runner is used as an important food fish (795), and is marketed either fresh or salted (791 855). Recruitment to the fishery occurs at age III (681 804).

Recreational: Blue runner is fished recreationally, primarily in the late spring and summer in coastal areas, from jetties and small boats (807). Recognized as a respectable game fish (49) and baitfish (795 1049). It is used extensively as bait fish along the southeast coast of the United States, especially for amberjack and sailfish (681 791 795). Sold as bait for snappers from April through September in northwest Florida (1049).

nodes.title: RANGE
nodes.body: Overall: This fish is widely distributed in the western Atlantic from Nova Scotia to southeast Brazil, in the Gulf of Mexico, and in the eastern Atlantic (363 788 795 804). The areas of greatest abundance of blue runner are the tropical waters along the southeast coast of the United States along the western side of the Gulf Stream and between the Florida current and the shore, throughout the West Indies, and seasonally throughout the Gulf of Mexico (363 795 801 804).

nodes.title: By State
nodes.body: Within Study Area: Distributed throughout the study area (788).

nodes.title: MOVEMENTS/MIGRATIONS
nodes.body: Larval and early juvenile: blue runner are carried northward by the Gulf Stream and Antilles Current. Juveniles 80-100 mm in length may migrate to inshore waters of the Atlantic coast or move eastward with the currents. Adults and juveniles favor the northern Gulf of Mexico during warm months (49). Adults and larger fish migrate southward or move offshore during colder months (December to June) (49 363 681). Adults probably migrate offshore during spawning season to reproduce (803).

nodes.title: LIFE MODE
nodes.body: This is a pelagic, fast-swimming species (804). Early life stages are planktonic. Late juveniles form small schools in and at the edges of the Florida Current (795). Adults usually form schools although larger individuals will remain solitary (806 803).

nodes.title: HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type: Blue runner is neritic and oceanic inhabiting primarily tropical and warm waters surrounding continents or large islands (795 804). Known as a schooling species (791 932). The larvae and juveniles inhabit offshore waters in association with the Gulf Stream (49). Larval blue runners are present in the Gulf Stream from May through November and are in greatest abundance from mid-June to mid-August. They are found throughout the Gulf, but greatest numbers occur in the central region (855). Juveniles are present in the upper 100 m of the water column in water depths of 180 m or greater (363). Individuals greater than 100 mm SL inhabit the shelf and near shore waters of the Atlantic coast, and almost all are taken in the upper 100m (49 363 795 804). Uncommon, if found at all, in Gulf estuaries (855 1049 1078 1079 1080).

Substrate: The blue runner has been observed in areas of shelly mud bottoms. In the Tampa Bay area, they have been seen over rocky reefs offshore (664). Early juveniles are often associated with floating objects such as sargassum or jellyfishes (363 681 805).

nodes.title: PHYSICAL /CHEMICAL
nodes.body:
Temperature: Larvae and juveniles have been taken at temperatures ranging from 20.4 to 29-4 C (46). Adults have been collected at temperatures from 20.0 to 30.8 C (795).

Salinity: Blue runners inhabit polyhaline to euhaline areas depending on life stage. Offshore spawning suggests that eggs occupy areas of full strength seawater (49). Larvae and juveniles occupy salinities ranging from 35.2 to 36.7 ppt (795). Adults have been taken in areas ranging from 26.0 to 36.2 ppt (49 224).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Repro Mode: External fertilization, viviparous.

Mating & Spawning: Based on the collection of larvae in the Gulf of Mexico, spawning occurs from January to August in offshore waters with a peak in the summer, but some evidence indicates spawning may occur year-round in some areas of the Gulf (795 803). Along the southeast Atlantic coast of the United States, spawning occurs early-April to early-September (49). The greatest period of activity occurs during June, July, and August (795 803). Larvae are most abundant in the Gulf Stream mid-June to mid-August (49 363 795 802), but are captured throughout the year in some areas of the Gulf (803). Spawning location, based on occurrence of larvae, is offshore and occurs in water depths from 10 to 183 m (49 855).

Reproductive capacity: Based on the examination of 25 individuals, fecundity ranged from 41,000 ova (243mm FL, 288 g) to 1,546,000 ova (383mm FL, 1,076 g) (803). Regression of fecundity on fork length (mm) was best fit by the curvilinear equation:
[eq]
Fecundity =.0000989 FL (Exp. 4.22) (r=.8, p=.01, df=9),
[/eq]
?while regression of fecundity on weight (g) was best fit by the linear equation:
[eq]
Fecundity = -152,000 + 986 (W) (r = -81, P = -01, df = 15) (803).
[/eq]

nodes.title: GROWTH & DEVELOPMENT
nodes.body:
Eggs: No information available.

Larvae: No information available.

Juveniles: The minimum size of a juvenile is 8.5 mm (363). The most noticeable changes in the structural development of a blue runner occur in two stages - between 8-12 mm and between 45-60 mm (795). Blue runner is a fast growing species. Approximately 75% of their maximum size is attained by age 11-111 (363 804).

Adults: Age-at-maturity size based on 185 fish taken in May-August in northwest Florida was less than or equal to 267mm FL (803). Males mature by a length of 225 mm, but females do not mature until approximately 247 mm (49). The largest recorded blue runner is 711 mm in length (363 804). Estimates of maximum weight approach 2,730 g. The blue runner is a moderately long-lived species with a life span up to 11 years possible. A growth equation for blue runner is:
[eq]
 	FL = 22.9 + (OR) 0.679815 (r = 0.86, a = 0.01)
[/eq]
where FL = fork length in mm and OR = otolith radius in units of 0.0071 mm (804).

Goodwin and Johnson (804) provided the following length-weight equation for combined
male and female specimens:

 	 W = 0.0000251355 (FL); n = 193, r = 0.98, P = 0.01

where W = weight in grams and FL = fork length in mm.

They found that this equation agreed well with that of Munro (1077) for Caribbean populations.

Using measurements from 193 fish from all size ranges, the equations for interconversion of fork length, standard length, and total length were (804):
[eq]
 	TL = -7.4792 + FL (1.1936); r = 1.0, P = 0.01
 	FL = 1.9453 + SL (1.0596); r = 1.0, P = 0.01
 	TL = -5.1694 + SL (1.2651; r = 0.99, P = 0.01
[/eq]
Length-at-age data were also presented by Goodwin and Johnson (804).

nodes.title: FOOD & FEEDING
nodes.body: Larval and early juvenile blue runners are carnivorous planktivores capable of foraging throughout the water column (795). Larvae forage almost entirely on cyclopoid copepods. After 8.5 mm, calanoid copepods are included in the diet. At lengths greater than 10.0 mm, the blue runner eats amphipods, larval fish, decapod larvae, ostracods, and fish eggs; however, copepods remain the main diet constituent (795). Adults feed primarily on fish (312 7911, but they also feed on shrimps, crabs and other invertebrates (791).

nodes.title: BIOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body: Factors Influencing Populations: Schools of carangid fish have been found in association with schools of red drum (529). Commercial fishermen use this knowledge to set nets for the sciaenids, and catch blue runner as well.

nodes.title: Persons Consulted
nodes.body: Ken Rice, Texas Parks & Wildlife, Coastal Fisheries, Brownsville, Texas. Page Cambell, Texas Parks & Wildlife, Coastal Fisheries, Rockport, Texas. Daniel R. Adams, Copano Causeway State Park, Rockport, Texas.

sections.heading: Revisions
sections.content:
January 19, 1993.  T.D. Phillips; Mote Marine Laboratory
FLELMR CODE: 1624

Scientific Name: Caranx crysos
Common Name: Blue Runner
OTHER COMMON NAMES: Jager boca, Bau, Deep water cavally; cavally, yellow mackerel (834); crevalle, hard tail, runner (312 834); horse crevalle, jurel, olbacore (834).

sections.heading: CLASSIFICATION
sections.content:
Phylum: Chordata
	Class: Osteichthyes
	Order: Perciformes
	Family: Carangidae

sections.heading: VALUE
sections.content:
Commercial: Blue runner is the most commercially important species of the jacks. A small historic fishery existed in the Chesapeake Bay, and along the Gulf Coast it has been reported to be ?esteemed as food? (312 834). Annual landings of blue runner in the northeast Gulf of Mexico are approximately 600 metric tons (804). The largest catches occur in the northwest and southeast coasts of Florida and off the Louisiana coast. Florida landings totaled 1.4 million pounds worth nearly $275,600 in 1982, with approximately 88% landed off the Florida west coast (902). Much of the Florida catch is used for bait, but some is sold fresh as food (791 1048). Beach and haul seines are the primary gear used to exploit blue runner (791). In Puerto Rico, Trinidad, and the West Indies, blue runner is used as an important food fish (795), and is marketed either fresh or salted (791 855). Recruitment to the fishery occurs at age III (681 804).

Recreational: Blue runner is fished recreationally, primarily in the late spring and summer in coastal areas, from jetties and small boats (807). Recognized as a respectable game fish (49) and baitfish (795 1049). It is used extensively as bait fish along the southeast coast of the United States, especially for amberjack and sailfish (681 791 795). Sold as bait for snappers from April through September in northwest Florida (1049).

sections.heading: RANGE
sections.content: Overall: This fish is widely distributed in the western Atlantic from Nova Scotia to southeast Brazil, in the Gulf of Mexico, and in the eastern Atlantic (363 788 795 804). The areas of greatest abundance of blue runner are the tropical waters along the southeast coast of the United States along the western side of the Gulf Stream and between the Florida current and the shore, throughout the West Indies, and seasonally throughout the Gulf of Mexico (363 795 801 804).

sections.heading: By State
sections.content: Within Study Area: Distributed throughout the study area (788).

sections.heading: MOVEMENTS/MIGRATIONS
sections.content: Larval and early juvenile: blue runner are carried northward by the Gulf Stream and Antilles Current. Juveniles 80-100 mm in length may migrate to inshore waters of the Atlantic coast or move eastward with the currents. Adults and juveniles favor the northern Gulf of Mexico during warm months (49). Adults and larger fish migrate southward or move offshore during colder months (December to June) (49 363 681). Adults probably migrate offshore during spawning season to reproduce (803).

sections.heading: LIFE MODE
sections.content: This is a pelagic, fast-swimming species (804). Early life stages are planktonic. Late juveniles form small schools in and at the edges of the Florida Current (795). Adults usually form schools although larger individuals will remain solitary (806 803).

sections.heading: HABITAT
sections.content:
Habitat Type: Blue runner is neritic and oceanic inhabiting primarily tropical and warm waters surrounding continents or large islands (795 804). Known as a schooling species (791 932). The larvae and juveniles inhabit offshore waters in association with the Gulf Stream (49). Larval blue runners are present in the Gulf Stream from May through November and are in greatest abundance from mid-June to mid-August. They are found throughout the Gulf, but greatest numbers occur in the central region (855). Juveniles are present in the upper 100 m of the water column in water depths of 180 m or greater (363). Individuals greater than 100 mm SL inhabit the shelf and near shore waters of the Atlantic coast, and almost all are taken in the upper 100m (49 363 795 804). Uncommon, if found at all, in Gulf estuaries (855 1049 1078 1079 1080).

Substrate: The blue runner has been observed in areas of shelly mud bottoms. In the Tampa Bay area, they have been seen over rocky reefs offshore (664). Early juveniles are often associated with floating objects such as sargassum or jellyfishes (363 681 805).

sections.heading: PHYSICAL /CHEMICAL
sections.content:
Temperature: Larvae and juveniles have been taken at temperatures ranging from 20.4 to 29-4 C (46). Adults have been collected at temperatures from 20.0 to 30.8 C (795).

Salinity: Blue runners inhabit polyhaline to euhaline areas depending on life stage. Offshore spawning suggests that eggs occupy areas of full strength seawater (49). Larvae and juveniles occupy salinities ranging from 35.2 to 36.7 ppt (795). Adults have been taken in areas ranging from 26.0 to 36.2 ppt (49 224).

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Repro Mode: External fertilization, viviparous.

Mating & Spawning: Based on the collection of larvae in the Gulf of Mexico, spawning occurs from January to August in offshore waters with a peak in the summer, but some evidence indicates spawning may occur year-round in some areas of the Gulf (795 803). Along the southeast Atlantic coast of the United States, spawning occurs early-April to early-September (49). The greatest period of activity occurs during June, July, and August (795 803). Larvae are most abundant in the Gulf Stream mid-June to mid-August (49 363 795 802), but are captured throughout the year in some areas of the Gulf (803). Spawning location, based on occurrence of larvae, is offshore and occurs in water depths from 10 to 183 m (49 855).

Reproductive capacity: Based on the examination of 25 individuals, fecundity ranged from 41,000 ova (243mm FL, 288 g) to 1,546,000 ova (383mm FL, 1,076 g) (803). Regression of fecundity on fork length (mm) was best fit by the curvilinear equation:
[eq]
Fecundity =.0000989 FL (Exp. 4.22) (r=.8, p=.01, df=9),
[/eq]
?while regression of fecundity on weight (g) was best fit by the linear equation:
[eq]
Fecundity = -152,000 + 986 (W) (r = -81, P = -01, df = 15) (803).
[/eq]

sections.heading: GROWTH & DEVELOPMENT
sections.content:
Eggs: No information available.

Larvae: No information available.

Juveniles: The minimum size of a juvenile is 8.5 mm (363). The most noticeable changes in the structural development of a blue runner occur in two stages - between 8-12 mm and between 45-60 mm (795). Blue runner is a fast growing species. Approximately 75% of their maximum size is attained by age 11-111 (363 804).

Adults: Age-at-maturity size based on 185 fish taken in May-August in northwest Florida was less than or equal to 267mm FL (803). Males mature by a length of 225 mm, but females do not mature until approximately 247 mm (49). The largest recorded blue runner is 711 mm in length (363 804). Estimates of maximum weight approach 2,730 g. The blue runner is a moderately long-lived species with a life span up to 11 years possible. A growth equation for blue runner is:
[eq]
 	FL = 22.9 + (OR) 0.679815 (r = 0.86, a = 0.01)
[/eq]
where FL = fork length in mm and OR = otolith radius in units of 0.0071 mm (804).

Goodwin and Johnson (804) provided the following length-weight equation for combined
male and female specimens:

 	 W = 0.0000251355 (FL); n = 193, r = 0.98, P = 0.01

where W = weight in grams and FL = fork length in mm.

They found that this equation agreed well with that of Munro (1077) for Caribbean populations.

Using measurements from 193 fish from all size ranges, the equations for interconversion of fork length, standard length, and total length were (804):
[eq]
 	TL = -7.4792 + FL (1.1936); r = 1.0, P = 0.01
 	FL = 1.9453 + SL (1.0596); r = 1.0, P = 0.01
 	TL = -5.1694 + SL (1.2651; r = 0.99, P = 0.01
[/eq]
Length-at-age data were also presented by Goodwin and Johnson (804).

sections.heading: FOOD & FEEDING
sections.content: Larval and early juvenile blue runners are carnivorous planktivores capable of foraging throughout the water column (795). Larvae forage almost entirely on cyclopoid copepods. After 8.5 mm, calanoid copepods are included in the diet. At lengths greater than 10.0 mm, the blue runner eats amphipods, larval fish, decapod larvae, ostracods, and fish eggs; however, copepods remain the main diet constituent (795). Adults feed primarily on fish (312 7911, but they also feed on shrimps, crabs and other invertebrates (791).

sections.heading: BIOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content: Factors Influencing Populations: Schools of carangid fish have been found in association with schools of red drum (529). Commercial fishermen use this knowledge to set nets for the sciaenids, and catch blue runner as well.
